study_identification_part.si4_title: Characterizing the heterogeneity of neurodegenerative diseases through EEG normative modeling

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To chart the aging trajectories of EEG spectral power and cortical source functional connectivity in healthy controls aged over 40 years, and to map the heterogeneity within Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD) groups using normative modeling.

rci7_preprocessing_pipeline.answer: MNE-Python for EEG preprocessing; pyprep (RANSAC-based bad channel detection); ICA with ICLabel for artifact removal; Autoreject for epoch cleaning; eLORETA for source reconstruction; Desikan-Killiany atlas (68 ROIs); amplitude envelope correlation (AEC) with pairwise orthogonalization; bandpass filtering (1-45 Hz for analysis); downsampling to 200 Hz (except dataset 12 at 160 Hz); common average reference; 10-second epochs
rci7_preprocessing_pipeline.reason: The Methods section provides comprehensive details about preprocessing and analysis pipelines. Data preprocessing included: bandpass filtering (1-100 Hz initially, then 1-45 Hz), downsampling to 200 Hz, notch filtering, bad channel detection/interpolation using pyprep RANSAC, common average reference, ICA with ICLabel for eye blink removal, 10-second epochs, and Autoreject for bad epoch detection. For source reconstruction: eLORETA was used, with age-specific head models, BEM method, 4098 sources per hemisphere (~5mm spacing), downsampled to 68 ROIs using Desikan-Killiany atlas. Connectivity computed using AEC with pairwise orthogonalization to reduce leakage. Spectral analysis used Welch's method with specific parameters. The paper cites using MNE-Python package for processing.
rci7_preprocessing_pipeline.supporting_text: The EEG preprocessing and artifact removal pipeline employed a multistage and automated algorithm, supported by visual inspection. Initially, EEG signals underwent bandpass filtering (1-100 Hz). All data signals were downsampled to a common frequency (200 Hz), except for dataset 12, which was originally sampled at 160 Hz ... A notch filter was applied to target the dataset-specific line frequency. Bad EEG channels were identified using the pyprep algorithm, which employs a RANSAC-based approach, and interpolated based on neighboring electrode data. ... rereferencing was applied using the common average reference method ... Eye blink artifacts were identified and rejected using Independent Component Analysis (ICA) the IClabel algorithm. A second bandpass filter (1-45 Hz) further refines the data. Then, EEG signals were segmented into 10-s epochs ... and the Autoreject toolbox was used to detect and clean or reject bad epochs. ... Cortical sources were estimated using the exact low-resolution brain electromagnetic tomography (eLORETA). ... Age-specific head models of the brain, skull, and scalp layers were built using an MRI template of elderly individuals aged 65-69 years, employing the Boundary Element Method (BEM) from the MNE Python package. The forward and inverse models were solved within a source space of 4098 sources per hemisphere, with approximately 5 mm spacing. ... We then downsampled the source space to 68 representative sources by averaging the sources within each region defined by the Desikan-Killiany atlas. Subsequently, we computed the functional connectivity between pairwise regions of interest, using the amplitude envelope correlation (AEC) method ... To mitigate zero-lag signal overlaps caused by spatial leakage, we applied a pairwise orthogonalization approach before computing connectivity.

nm4_response_variable.answer: Two types of EEG features: (1) Relative spectral power at scalp electrodes (19 channels from 10-20 montage) across five frequency bands (delta 1-4 Hz, theta 4-8 Hz, alpha 8-13 Hz, beta 13-30 Hz, gamma 30-45 Hz); (2) Functional connectivity at cortical source level (68 ROIs from Desikan-Killiany atlas, yielding 2278 pairwise connections) across the same five frequency bands, computed using amplitude envelope correlation (AEC)
nm4_response_variable.reason: The Methods section clearly describes both response variables modeled. For spectral features: 'we initially focused on the spectral features of the EEG signal as the designated response variable' with 'Relative power in specific frequency bands (delta [1-4 Hz], theta [4-8 Hz], alpha [8-13 Hz], beta [13-30 Hz], gamma [30-45 Hz])' computed at 19 scalp electrodes from standardized 10-20 montage. For connectivity features: source-level functional connectivity was computed with 'We then downsampled the source space to 68 representative sources by averaging the sources within each region defined by the Desikan-Killiany atlas' and 'we computed the functional connectivity between pairwise regions of interest, using the amplitude envelope correlation (AEC) method'. The Results section states 'relative EEG power and cortical source functional connectivity values were computed' as response variables.
nm4_response_variable.supporting_text: In this study, we initially focused on the spectral features of the EEG signal as the designated response variable. ... Relative power in specific frequency bands (delta [1-4 Hz], theta [4-8 Hz], alpha [8-13 Hz], beta [13-30 Hz], gamma [30-45 Hz]) is computed by dividing the absolute power within each narrow band by the total power of the broader band [1-45 Hz]. For scalp-level spectral analysis, we downsampled the electrode configurations to a common 10-20 montage to account for the variability in the number of channels across datasets. We used the 'Nihon Kohden EEG 2100' as the reference because it has the minimal number of channels (19 electrodes) among the systems used ... We then downsampled the source space to 68 representative sources by averaging the sources within each region defined by the Desikan-Killiany atlas. Subsequently, we computed the functional connectivity between pairwise regions of interest, using the amplitude envelope correlation (AEC) method ... Specifically, relative EEG power and cortical source functional connectivity values were computed at each scalp electrode/functional connection between cortical source pairs for the frequency bands of interest (i.e., delta, theta, alpha, beta, and gamma) were modeled.

nm7_nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study addresses some but not all aspects of nuisance structure. Addressed: (1) Age nonlinearity - fractional polynomials used to model nonlinear age effects; (2) Heteroscedasticity - GAMLSS framework models variance (sigma) as function of age for connectivity features; (3) Non-Gaussian distributions - empirically selected optimal distribution families (SEP4, GG, ST3, ST1) for each feature/band; (4) Multi-site effects - site evaluated as covariate (fixed and random) during model selection, though not retained in final models; standardized preprocessing including downsampling to common montage for spectral analysis; LOSO validation showed robustness (r>0.88 for spectral, r>0.90 for FC). Not fully addressed: (1) No explicit batch-removal harmonization (ComBat, etc.); (2) QC metrics (motion artifacts, signal quality) handled via preprocessing exclusion but not included as covariates in normative models; (3) Different EEG systems with varying channel numbers (19-256) addressed through standardization but may introduce variability; (4) Sex effects only partially modeled (included in delta connectivity mu only). The paper acknowledges in limitations: 'data gathered from 14 distinct spontaneous EEG studies, each using different EEG systems with varying spatial resolutions (19, 32, 64, 128, 256 channels) and protocols that were not harmonized' and mentions 'Future research should explore advanced harmonization techniques, such as Combat family methods'.
nm7_nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: Model covariates beyond age, including sex and site (considered both as a fixed effect and a random effect), are empirically selected. Each covariate is sequentially incorporated into the parameter formulas, and the resulting models are compared based on their BIC scores. ... GAMLSS are semi-parametric regression models offering a flexible framework for capturing complex relationships. They assume a specific distribution for the response variable, with parameters linked to a set of explanatory variables through linear or nonlinear predictor functions. ... The GAMLSS framework provides an extensive range of distribution families. Here, we used an empirical approach to determine the most suitable distribution, by training models across all considered distribution families (with 3 or more moments, continuous/mixed), and comparing them using the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC). ... Following Bethlehem et al., we used fractional polynomials as a smoothing function to accommodate nonlinearity while maintaining model stability. ... Our data was gathered from 14 distinct spontaneous EEG studies, each using different EEG systems with varying spatial resolutions (19, 32, 64, 128, 256 channels) and protocols that were not harmonized. To standardize our analysis for scalp spectral analysis of EEG activity, we mapped all systems to a common low spatial resolution (19 channels). ... Future research should explore advanced harmonization techniques, such as Combat family methods to further enhance compatibility across diverse EEG systems.

nm8_nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The study performed extensive validation on the training data and using non-independent resampling methods. Specifically: (1) Model performance assessed via residual diagnostics on training data - 'To evaluate the performance of our models, we examined the normalized quantile residuals' with visual inspection showing 'residuals plotted against the fitted values and the index were evenly scattered around the horizontal line at 0' and 'normal quantile-quantile (Q-Q) plots showed an approximately linear trend' (Supplementary Figs. 3-4); (2) Leave-one-study-out (LOSO) cross-validation performed - 'To validate the robustness of the model, we conducted a series of leave-one-study-out analyses. Specifically, we systematically excluded one dataset from the primary datasets, refitted the GAMLSS models, evaluated all model parameters, and then extracted developmental trajectories' with results showing 'remarkable consistency, with a very high correlation between the trajectories derived from the primary full dataset and those from the subsets (all r > 0.88 for spectral features, all r > 0.90 for FC features)' (Supplementary Figs. 5-6). These validations used the training data (400 HC) with resampling, making them non-independent validations.
nm8_nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: To evaluate the performance of our models, we examined the normalized quantile residuals. Visual inspection of the residual plots depicted in Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4 suggests that our models exhibit adequate fit and quality. Specifically, the residuals plotted against the fitted values and the index were evenly scattered around the horizontal line at 0. The kernel density estimation of the residuals displayed an approximate normal distribution, and the normal quantile-quantile (Q-Q) plots showed an approximately linear trend with an intercept of 0 and a slope of 1. To validate the robustness of the model, we conducted a series of leave-one-study-out analyses. Specifically, we systematically excluded one dataset from the primary datasets, refitted the GAMLSS models, evaluated all model parameters, and then extracted developmental trajectories. We then compared these alternative trajectories to those derived from the 14 datasets for each feature and frequency band. Our findings showed remarkable consistency, with a very high correlation between the trajectories derived from the primary full dataset and those from the subsets (all r > 0.88 for spectral features, all r > 0.90 for FC features), even when large datasets were excluded

nm9_nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The study implemented a proper train-test split validation strategy with held-out independent data from the same domain. The Methods section states: 'Our cohort consisted of 933 individuals, subdivided into a group of healthy controls (N = 400 in the training set, N = 99 in the held-out testing set)' and the Results section confirms 'Normative models were trained on 400 (46% M) HC participants while 99 (42% M) HC participants were held out as a comparison group against the clinical cohort'. The normative model parameters were estimated exclusively on the 400 training HC, then the 99 held-out HC were projected onto these models to derive deviation scores. The Methods describes: 'we trained GAMLSS models for each channel/connection across all frequency bands using the healthy control training group HC(train) (80% of the healthy sample). This is proper independent same-domain validation with 80/20 split and normative parameters fit only on training data.

nm10_nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The study did not perform validation on an external dataset from a different domain. All validation was conducted within the same multi-site cohort: training on 400 HC (80%), testing on 99 HC (20%) from the same 14-site dataset, and applying to clinical patients (PD and AD) from the same datasets. The leave-one-study-out (LOSO) analysis excluded individual datasets iteratively but refitted models each time on the remaining data, rather than applying a pre-trained model to a truly external independent dataset from different cohorts/sites. The paper does not mention application to any external validation cohort or different-domain dataset. Additionally, for each channel and location, we calculated the percentage of subjects showing extreme deviations at this specific location among those with at least one extreme deviation, which resulted in group-specific overlap maps. ... we used the patient-specific deviations to compute a new metric called EDI (extreme deviations index) defined as the averaged EEG source connectivity of the extremely deviated solutions. clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Group comparisons between clinical groups (PD, AD) and held-out healthy controls (HC test) using Mann-Whitney U tests for number of extreme deviations per subject across frequency bands (p < 0.05, p < 0.01 significance levels reported); group-based permutation tests (5000 permutations) for channel-wise and connection-wise overlap maps with false discovery rate (FDR) correction (p < 0.05); comparison of percentage of subjects with at least one extreme deviation across groups; spatial overlap analysis calculating proportion of subjects with extreme deviations at each location among those with at least one extreme deviation; Spearman correlations between patient-specific deviation metrics (EDI and z-EDI) and clinical assessments (UPDRS for PD motor severity, MMSE for cognitive function); significant correlations found: PD UPDRS with EDI delta band negative (ρ = 0.24, p = 0.0254, n = 86); PD MMSE with EDI delta band negative (ρ = -0.35, p = 0.0000, n = 182), alpha and gamma bands; AD MMSE with EDI delta band negative (ρ = -0.26, p = 0.0107, n = 146); PD MMSE with z-EDI theta and beta bands; network-level analysis showing distribution of significantly deviated connections across resting-state networks (DMN, DAN, etc.)
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: EEG normative modeling revealed significant heterogeneity in PD and AD patients with approximately 30% showing spectral deviations and approximately 80% showing functional connectivity deviations; spatial overlap of deviant features was low (≤60% for spectral, ≤25% for connectivity), indicating substantial individual variability; patient-specific deviations correlated with clinical severity (PD UPDRS ρ=0.24, p=0.025; AD MMSE ρ=-0.26, p=0.01).
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Using GAMLSS normative modeling on EEG data from 499 healthy controls, the study generated age-related trajectories for spectral power and cortical source functional connectivity across five frequency bands. When 237 PD and 197 AD patients were projected onto these models, significant heterogeneity emerged: approximately 30% of patients exhibited spectral power deviations (highest at theta band: PD 31.36%, AD 27.41% positive deviation; beta band: PD 12.71%, AD 23.35% negative deviation), while approximately 80% showed functional connectivity deviations (PD negative deviations reached 86.86% at delta band). Spatial overlap analysis revealed low consistency: ≤60% overlap for spectral features and ≤25% for connectivity features, indicating substantial individual variability within disease groups. Group-based permutation tests (FDR p<0.05) identified significant differences: PD showed common fronto-central deviations at delta band and central deviations at theta/beta; AD showed temporal-parietal deviations at beta band. For connectivity, significantly deviated connections predominantly involved the default mode network (DMN: approximately 35-44% across bands for both diseases) and dorsal attention network. Patient-specific Extreme Deviation Index (EDI) correlated significantly with clinical measures: PD motor severity (UPDRS) with delta band EDI (ρ=0.24, p=0.025, n=86), PD cognitive function (MMSE) with delta band EDI (ρ=-0.35, p<0.001, n=182) and alpha/gamma bands, and AD cognitive function (MMSE) with delta band EDI (ρ=-0.26, p=0.01, n=146). Leave-one-study-out validation demonstrated model robustness (r>0.88 for spectral, r>0.90 for connectivity across dataset exclusions).

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Sample size not reaching scale of major MRI initiatives with imbalanced age distribution (primarily 60-70 years, limited data above 72 years); multi-site data from 14 studies using non-harmonized EEG systems with varying spatial resolutions (19-256 channels) potentially introducing variability; downsampling to 19 channels for standardization may overlook information from higher-resolution setups; heterogeneity within patient groups regarding disease stages (MCI vs dementia) not fully characterized; lack of biomarker data (CSF, amyloid PET) for neuropathological confirmation; medication effects not comprehensively investigated as covariates; use of fixed frequency bands rather than individual alpha frequency peaks; limited exploration of correlations with clinical variables (symptom profiles, illness duration, disease severity)
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: First, while our sample size is substantial for EEG studies (n approximately 933), it does not reach the scale often seen in the most important international MRI and fMRI initiatives, and it may not be fully representative of the general population. Notably, in this study, EEG data collected from HC participants primarily fall within the age range (60-70 years), with a notable lack of EEG data above 72 years. ... Our data was gathered from 14 distinct spontaneous EEG studies, each using different EEG systems with varying spatial resolutions (19, 32, 64, 128, 256 channels) and protocols that were not harmonized. To standardize our analysis for scalp spectral analysis of EEG activity, we mapped all systems to a common low spatial resolution (19 channels). While this approach minimize variability across datasets, it may overlook some relevant information available from higher spatial resolution setups. ... Moreover, this study did not include biomarker data (e.g., cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, amyloid PET scans) for neurodegeneration diagnoses, which were based on clinical criteria. ... Additionally, this study did not comprehensively investigate correlations between EEG findings and clinically relevant variables, such as symptom profiles, age of onset, illness duration, medication exposure, or disease severity across disorders.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: Study introduced Extreme Deviation Index (EDI) as patient-specific marker for clinical assessment, defined as averaged connectivity values over extremely deviated connections, showing significant correlations with clinical measures; z-EDI variant (averaged z-scores) also computed and correlated with clinical assessments; separate analysis of positive vs negative deviations provided directional interpretation (e.g., patients showing increased vs decreased connectivity/power relative to normative model); network-level attribution of deviations showing predominance of DMN and DAN involvement; exploratory medication subgroup analysis for PD patients (ON vs OFF medication comparisons, Supplementary Figs 19-22) showing no significant differences but limited by small OFF-medication sample (n=19); spatial overlap maps quantified consistency across individuals, revealing greater variability in connectivity than spectral features; sex-stratified exploratory analyses examining differences in EEG features between males and females within each group (Supplementary Figs 1-2, Tables 1-2); comprehensive data availability with 7 of 14 datasets openly accessible (OpenNeuro, OSF, Zenodo platforms) and code available on GitHub (https://github.com/MINDIG-1/NM-neurodeg)

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is one of the first large-scale EEG normative modeling studies for neurodegenerative diseases (following prior work by Lefebvre et al. 2018 for autism and Ebadi et al. 2024 for pediatric psychiatric disorders by the same group). The study emphasizes heterogeneity mapping rather than group-level biomarker discovery, aligning with Precision Medicine principles. Multi-site aggregation (14 datasets) represents substantial coordination effort with diverse international collaborators (Greece, Germany, Switzerland, USA, France, Turkey, Lebanon, Finland, Norway, Denmark). Diagnostic criteria were standardized: AD diagnosed per NINCDS-ADRDA and DSM criteria; PD diagnosed per UKPDSBB criteria or MDS clinical criteria. Clinical assessments included UPDRS for PD motor severity, MMSE for cognitive function, with availability varying by dataset (UPDRS: 86 PD patients; MMSE: 182 PD, 146 AD patients). The study explicitly discusses medication status as important consideration: 92% of PD patients (218/237) were ON medication during recordings, reflecting typical daily conditions; exploratory analyses found no significant medication effects but sample limitations noted. Age-specific head models (65-69 years template) were used for source reconstruction, appropriate for the older adult population studied. The study used standard frequency band definitions rather than individual alpha frequency adjustment, which may not optimally capture individual differences in peak alpha frequency (acknowledged limitation). Leave-one-study-out validation demonstrated robustness despite heterogeneous data sources. The paper positions EEG normative modeling as complementary to existing MRI-based approaches, offering advantages of cost, accessibility, and temporal resolution for functional brain assessment. Authors plan future work on: (1) incorporating longitudinal data for trajectory characterization; (2) using deviation scores for disease subtype/stage classification following Young et al. 2018 approach; (3) including additional covariates like education and socioeconomic factors; (4) biomarker integration for neuropathological validation; (5) advanced harmonization techniques like ComBat. Ethical approval obtained from all 14 local institutional review boards with informed consent from all participants or legal guardians. This study represents MINDIG company R&D activity with funding from Region Bretagne and Rennes Metropole.
